findings.summary: DockerCommandLineCodeExecutor is created but never started; code execution crashes with ValueError
findings.failure_scenario: User calls MagenticOne(client=client) without specifying code_executor on a system with Docker available. The team is created successfully via _create_default_code_executor() returning an unstarted DockerCommandLineCodeExecutor. When the Orchestrator later delegates code execution, CodeExecutorAgent.execute_code_block() calls self._code_executor.execute_code_blocks(), which reaches _execute_code_dont_check_setup() at DockerCommandLineCodeExecutor line 332, which checks 'if self._container is None or not self._running' and raises ValueError('Container is not running. Must first be started with either start or a context manager.'). The executor.__init__ only stores configuration; the Docker container is only created in its async start() method, which nothing in the call chain (MagenticOne.__init__ -> CodeExecutorAgent.__init__ -> BaseGroupChat.run_stream) ever calls.

findings.summary: Bare 'except Exception: pass' silently swallows Docker executor construction failures and falls through to a misleading warning claiming Docker is unavailable
findings.failure_scenario: Docker is installed and running, but DockerCommandLineCodeExecutor() raises an exception during construction (e.g., a disk-full error creating the work dir, or a bug in a dependency). The bare 'except Exception: pass' at line 58 swallows the error completely. Execution falls through to lines 62-68 which emit a UserWarning stating 'Docker is not available or not running... install Docker.' The user is misled into thinking they need to install Docker, and the actual construction error is never reported.

findings.summary: Docstring example for the default constructor path is misleading and leads users to a runtime crash
findings.failure_scenario: A user follows the docstring example on line 130: 'm1 = MagenticOne(client=client)  # Uses DockerCommandLineCodeExecutor by default'. The comment implies this is correct and safe. But this path creates an unstarted Docker executor (see finding 1), so when the user later calls m1.run_stream(task=task), code execution fails with ValueError. The docstring is the first code many users will copy-paste, leading them directly into the crash.

findings.summary: Unreachable 'return False' at end of _is_docker_available() is dead code
findings.failure_scenario: Given the module-level import logic, when _docker_available is True, docker is guaranteed to be non-None. All code paths before line 49 either return True (successful ping), return False (DockerException caught), or are unreachable (docker is None when _docker_available is True is impossible). This dead code confuses maintainers and may mask bugs if the import logic changes in the future.

findings.summary: docker_tests_enabled() creates a Docker client via docker.from_env() but never closes it, leaking connections
findings.failure_scenario: The docker_tests_enabled() helper creates a Docker client (line 26: client = docker.from_env()) and calls client.ping() but never calls client.close(). Each invocation leaks a connection. This function is called from @pytest.mark.skipif decorators (evaluated at collection time) and from test assertions. On systems with Docker connection limits or when running test collection many times, this can exhaust available connections.

findings.summary: test_docker_availability_check tests the test-file-local helper instead of the production _is_docker_available function
findings.failure_scenario: test_docker_availability_check() at line 70 calls _is_docker_available(), which at line 33 is redefined in the test file as a thin wrapper around docker_tests_enabled(). The actual production function at autogen_ext.teams.magentic_one._is_docker_available() has real Docker connection logic (docker.from_env(), client.ping(), DockerException handling) that is never directly tested by this test case. A bug in the production function's Docker connectivity logic would not be caught.
